verdict_reason: Abstract figures are clear and self-consistent, and the page is a Wikipedia-sourced stub with no empirical content on OPEC's welfare effects. One attributed paragraph (B-claim, unrefereed) fits. It is a market-power/cartel paper, not a land-rent paper, so it earns no NEW research page and no resource-rents.md edit beyond a possible See Also; the benefit is a contrast between cartel rent (restricted output, inefficiency) and scarcity rent. claim_grade: B, Tier 1 (NBER working paper by recognised scholars; Asker/Collard-Wexler/De Loecker are established IO/empirical economists; none are in people-tiers.json, so judged by rubric). content_summary: Abstract (w36058 page): framework quantifying welfare impact of coordinated cartel production decisions 'while allowing for other distortions'; contrasts a 'marginal' and an 'infra-marginal' welfare loss with a 'naive approach that fails to recognize the existence of other distortions operating alongside market power'. Applied to OPEC in global crude oil using 'unique micro data on cost and production' to quantify deadweight loss and productive inefficiency. 'From 1970 onward, the naive approach implies that OPEC generated 2.2 trillion dollars of welfare losses, two-thirds from productive inefficiency and one-third from deadweight loss.' So roughly $1.5T productive inefficiency and $0.7T deadweight loss (derived arithmetic, not stated in abstract). 'Eliminating cost-minimization violations outside the cartel shrinks losses to around 0.7 trillion dollars', i.e. other frictions are 'complementary to OPEC's market power'. NOT stated in the abstract: price basis (real vs nominal, base year), end year of the period, the exact meaning of 'other distortions' beyond 'cost-minimization violations outside the cartel' (apparently non-cartel producers not producing at minimum cost, e.g. state-owned or otherwise distorted producers), whether the ~$0.7T is the marginal or infra-marginal measure, and how it splits. The ~$0.7T is also coincidentally the same size as the DWL third of the naive figure; do not conflate. The framing 'naive' versus corrected is the authors'.

suggested_text: In a 2026 NBER working paper (unrefereed), Asker, Collard-Wexler, De Cannière and De Loecker estimate the welfare cost of OPEC's market power using micro data on production costs. Under what they call a naive approach that ignores other distortions in the oil market, OPEC generated about $2.2 trillion of welfare losses from 1970 onward, roughly two-thirds from productive inefficiency and one-third from deadweight loss; once cost-minimization violations by producers outside the cartel are eliminated, the estimated loss falls to around $0.7 trillion, which the authors read as showing that other frictions in the oil market are complementary to OPEC's market power. The estimates measure the cost of restricting supply, a different matter from the scarcity rent that oil in the ground would yield under any ownership regime. Source line (Sources only): Asker, Collard-Wexler, De Cannière & De Loecker, NBER WP 36058 (Nov 2026), doi:10.3386/w36058; full text not accessible at last review (2026-11-23); summary rests on the abstract; unrefereed (B-claim).

content_summary: Abstract (w36055 page): Setting: Dallas County administrative property-tax records linked with voting records. Survey: 'Americans, on average, believe Republican homeowners are more likely to appeal their property taxes than Democratic homeowners with similarly valued homes.' Result: 'the partisan gap in appeals is small, both in absolute terms (0.29 percentage points) and relative to several demographic gaps in appeals we use as benchmarks.' Motives: 'Using quasi-experimental and field experimental evidence, we find that Democrats and Republicans appeal for broadly similar reasons.' Conclusion: 'strikingly similar in both their propensity to appeal ... and their underlying motives.' Disclosures: experiments approved by the IRB at the University of Texas at Dallas; generative AI used for survey development, data analysis and copyediting; 'Parts of this study were originally in another working paper (NBER WP No. 27816, posted in September 2020).' NOT in the abstract: sign of the 0.29 pp gap (which party appeals more), baseline appeal rate, which demographic benchmarks (education, race, age, income, home value etc.) and their sizes, sample size, years, the survey's sample/size, the quasi-experiment's identification strategy, which field experiment(s) (likely the mailed-guide experiment later cited as Nathan et al. 2025, unconfirmed), and the specific motives tested. Do not name these.

suggested_text: A companion Dallas County study by Nathan, Perez-Truglia and Zentner (NBER Working Paper 36055, 2026, unrefereed) links property-tax appeal records to voting records and reports that the partisan gap in appeal rates is small, 0.29 percentage points, and smaller than several demographic gaps used as benchmarks; it also reports, from quasi-experimental and field-experimental evidence, that Democrats and Republicans appeal for broadly similar reasons, although survey respondents expected Republican homeowners to appeal more. The authors' results concern who appeals, not whether appeals improve assessment accuracy. See Also entry: [Nathan, Perez-Truglia & Zentner on partisanship and appeals] linked to the NBER page.
